title: Don't hurry your tongue
hook: don't move your tongue to hurry the revelation; its collecting is on Us (75:16–17)

segments.voice: Yesterday: lawwamah, and your line, the voice that blames. Did you listen to it, and do the small thing it asked? Today, the same surah, and a moment in the middle of revelation itself. Day six hundred fifty-eight, the end of a week.

Have you ever tried to take notes while someone was talking too fast? You scribble, you whisper the words to yourself, you fall behind, and you lose the next sentence because you were still holding the last one. Now raise the stakes: the words are revelation, and losing even one is unthinkable. In surah al-Qiyamah, in the middle of verses about the Last Day, the Qur'an suddenly turns and speaks to the Prophet about exactly that: his lips, moving too fast.

Verses sixteen and seventeen, in Pickthall's translation: "Stir not thy tongue herewith to hasten it. Lo! upon Us (resteth) the putting together thereof and the reading thereof." The story behind it is in the first pages of Sahih al-Bukhari. Ibn 'Abbas explained that when revelation came, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ found it heavy, and he would move his lips, repeating the words as they came, for fear of forgetting them. And then Ibn 'Abbas did something lovely: he moved his own lips, to show his student how the Prophet had done it. His student, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, did the same for the next generation. A gesture handed down like a family recipe. Then these verses came. Don't rush. Collecting it in your heart, and its recitation, are Our responsibility. Verse eighteen: when We recite it, follow its recitation. Verse nineteen: then its explanation is on Us too. After this, Ibn 'Abbas said, when Jibril came, the Prophet would listen. And when Jibril left, he would recite it as it had been recited to him. Notice the shape of it. First listen. Then speak. The memory wasn't his burden to carry by force. It would be given. Surah Ta Ha has a similar line: don't be in haste with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say, my Lord, increase me in knowledge. There's something here for anyone who learns anything. The fear of forgetting can make you grab so hard that you stop listening. The verse says: let go of the grabbing, and listen all the way to the end.
screen: `STIR NOT THY TONGUE TO HASTEN IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: slow your recitation. If you know a short surah or prayer, don't say it yet. First, listen to it in your mind, all the way through, without moving your lips. Then, when it's finished, recite it once, the way it came to you. If you don't know one, do the same with any line you love. Listen first. Speak second. Notice how different it feels to not be chasing the words. The bell holds the time.
Jibril. In 75:16–17 the Prophet is told not to rush the revelation he hears from Jibril: first listen, then recite, since gathering it is Allah's to keep. Today's word.

Your line: don't hurry. This week ran from stand in the night, slowly measured, what is easy, arise, give don't count, and the voice that blames, to here. Today, in one conversation, let the other person finish completely before you speak. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: One way Muslims learn the Qur'an is to listen to a teacher's recitation first and then repeat it, a method that echoes 75:16–19 and Ibn 'Abbas's account of how the Prophet received revelation.

fork.reveal: don't hurry your tongue. listen, follow the recitation, and its collecting and explanation are on Allah.

original.note: Arabic, 75:16: don't move your tongue with it (to hurry it).

trapdoor: what it means: the Prophet was told to stop rushing the words of revelation; listening first, the memory would be given.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari's fifth hadith preserves Ibn 'Abbas moving his lips, shown to his student; 75:16–19 assigns gathering, recitation and explanation to Allah.
